session_title: Further Sharing of Literary Adaptations into Film and Television
theme: 影视-分享更多的文学改编影视

content.text: Just finished watching the show, and this scene really brought tears to my eyes. It reminds me of what you mentioned last time when we discussed "A Lifelong Journey"—the technique of conveying emotions through material details, which is also masterfully employed here.

This scene is truly moving, and the actor's performance is incredibly nuanced. Just as we previously reviewed the "period texture" in "A Lifelong Journey," a great performance allows the audience to touch the inner world of the characters.

Yes, and I always feel like this actor looks familiar, as if I've seen him somewhere before. This sense of déjà vu is a bit like when we first saw your grandfather's bronze lock—it always felt like there was a story hidden behind it.

Is this the scene? I checked, and this actor has indeed performed in many profound works. It reminds me of the "resonance of craftsmanship" you mentioned when we shared the indigo-dyed tea set earlier. A good actor can also leave a unique texture in different roles.

Yes, that's it! I remember now—it's a still from the movie *Dying to Survive*. The profound depiction of social reality in it shares a similar essence with the 'investigation of era-specific details' we discussed in Session 7. Both use specific stories to bridge the past and the present.

Her acting skills are truly impressive; she is a very capable actress. This reminds me of our previous discussion on 'individual narratives'—whether it's the health diary of old tea or the creative story behind the indigo-dyed tea ceremony, every detail carries a unique life experience.

This is her profile, you can take a look. While organizing it, I felt as if I were writing an 'excavation' report for your grandfather's bronze lock—requiring meticulous research to record all the experiences worth remembering.

No wonder the performance is so vivid; it turns out the experience is so rich. Just as you said before, sincerity is often hidden in the smallest traces. The accumulation of this actor in different works has become the foundation of her performance. This reminds me of when we were making Qingtuan, and you consulted the elderly for traditional precautions. That meticulousness now seems very valuable.

I'd like to watch more film and television adaptations of this kind of literature. Do you have any recommendations? Ever since we discussed the woven baskets and fabric patterns in "A Lifelong Journey," I've been particularly fascinated by this way of storytelling through visual elements.

Yes, I've compiled a list, all based on literary works, some of which retain the charm of the original texts. The process of compiling it was a bit like our previous division of labor in making Qingtuan—it required screening, comparing, and finding those works that best embody the "warmth of paper" and "historical continuity."

This list includes several works for your reference. I've specifically noted the adaptation features of each piece, much like when I shared the guide on making green rice balls with you before. I hope this information helps you better 'savor the flavor.'

Great, I'll go check it out now. By the way, regarding the green rice cake you mentioned earlier, when we meet up this weekend, could we chat about these films and shows while we enjoy it? Just like we planned for our first offline meet-up, in a bookstore with that "warm, paper-filled atmosphere," taking our time to savor it would be really nice.

Of course, just as we previously discussed old objects and handicrafts, we can savor them slowly. From exploring the flavors of spring's green rice cakes, to the "excavation" report on old copper locks, and then to sharing the experience of a blue-dyed tea ceremony, our conversations always find depth in the rhythm of "slow living."

Hmm, I think in some of these adaptations, using voiceovers for inner monologues actually breaks the immersion of the visuals, while other empty shots are more powerful than straightforward dialogue. This reminds me of the photo you shared of Mo Dian dozing off by the windowsill—that kind of silent companionship sometimes conveys emotions better than any words.

Yes, this reminds me of the era details we discussed earlier, such as hand-woven baskets and fabric patterns, which convey emotions and historical continuity through visual elements. Just like Old Tea's quirk—only sleeping in an old rattan chair—such stubborn details themselves tell a story.

Yes, just like the health records of the old tea you shared—those details, though silent, carry profound memories. From Session 6, when you started documenting its condition, to now, as we discuss film and television, I always feel that what we focus on are those easily overlooked yet incredibly precious "textures of life."

The same holds true for film and television works, which connect the past with the present through artistic choices, allowing us to find resonance in a slower-paced life. This aligns with our motivation to preserve old objects and revive traditional crafts—both are acts of resisting the fading of memory and building archives of personal and collective recollections.

Well said. I'm looking forward to the weekend gathering, where we can not only taste handmade green rice balls but also delve deeper into these cultural topics. Starting from Session 1, when we planned to make green rice balls together, each offline meeting has enriched our 'shared narrative.'

Me too. It makes me feel that our conversation has evolved from initially exploring the taste of Qingtuan to delving into broader cultural dimensions. Just like that late Qing Dynasty copper lock, it started as a specific object and extended into discussions about protection, inheritance, and personal narratives.

Yes, from the springtime green rice balls to the vintage items, and then to film and TV show sharing, each step feels like weaving a shared story. I'll start watching the works on the list right away, thank you for your recommendations! Remember to bring your sweet-filled green rice balls this weekend, and I'll have my savory ones ready. Let's continue this 'cultural roots journey' that has been ongoing since March.
